newsitem.title: TURKEY: SOCCER SHOWCASE-TURKISH TOP-DOGS RENEW LONG-STANDING RIVALRY.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-TURKISH TOP-DOGS RENEW LONG-STANDING RIVALRY.

text.p: When Graeme Souness planted Galatasaray's red-and-yellow flag in the centre circle of Istanbul rival Fenerbahce's pitch last year, he was shocked at the intensity of the reaction by furious Fenerbahce fans.

Violence erupted on the stands at Souness's action, which followed Galatasaray's victory over Fenerbahce in the Turkish Cup final, and fans threw bottles at President Suleyman Demirel as he presented the trophy.
Souness, since replaced as Galatasaray coach, was carpeted for ungentlemanly conduct.
He should have known that when he posted the flag in an exuberant victory flourish that he was stirring up the bitterest and most ancient rivalry of Turkish soccer history.
Galatasaray and Fenerbahce, currently first and second in the standings and who meet on Sunday, have been undisputed top dogs of Turkish soccer since they first met in 1909.

They have played each other an astonishing 326 times. Fenerbahce now have the edge with 121 wins against 104 by Galatasaray, but it took them five years to record their first victory -- and first goal.
The blue-and-yellow club, which claims to have 25 million supporters in a country of 55 million people, wants another win on Sunday to move level with the old enemy on 47 points.
"We will send our arch-rival Galatasaray back with no points. We will definitely become leaders," said a confident Fenerbahce deputy chairman Vefa Kucuk.
And the odds seem to be in favour of Fenerbahce.
The club trounced Galatasaray 4-0 on the hallowed home turf of the Ali Sami Yen stadium in its last match in September and has the meanest defence in the league, conceding just 11 goals in 20 games.

However, despite filling the top two places in the standings, both clubs have been off form in the second half of the season. Galatasaray have drawn all three of their post-break games, scoring just one goal, while Fenerbahce's last outing was a disappointing goalless draw at lowly Altay.

Some people say the hostility between the clubs is intensified because the Bosphorus splits their grounds. For one thing, escaping Galatasaray fans are easy prey for Fenerbahce supporters on the rampage as they can be caught up while trying to board boats or cross the crammed Bosphorus Bridge.
Bellicose remarks by Fenerbahce chairman Ali Sen, who speaks in terms of "enemies", have recently inflamed the rivalry further.
But the Turkish soccer federation has clamped down, banning Sen from conducting official club business and banishing him from the directors' box for two months for insulting a referee.
The punishment appeared to calm Sen somewhat as he warned players to stop swearing at referees and issued a ban on speaking to the media.
But when a similar ban on Galatasaray coach Fatih Terim was reversed, Fenerbahce issued a declaration condemning the decision.

"Fenerbahce's declaration is a real sign of weakness," said Galatasaray spokesman Ates Unal Erzen. "Rather than wasting their energy writing a declaration they should try and get their men to play soccer."

It is not just Sen's fervour that has divided the clubs so bitterly. Back in 1934, a match between the two sides was abandoned after a fight broke out between the players which resulted in various punishments for 17 of them, including a life ban for the Fenerbahce goalkeeper.
However, there have been rare moments of camaraderie. After drawing in the final of the Prime Minister's Cup in 1958, the teams decided to share the title - and cut the trophy down the middle.

Lately, the players have been good friends off the pitch, since the two clubs virtually make up the entire national squad that made it for the first time to the European championship finals in England last year.
According to the Fanatik sports daily, Souness, now manger of English Premier League Southampton, declined a Galatasaray invitation to watch Sunday's match.
But he did send his old club a good luck message: "Think of how we toppled Fenerbahce that day and play with that attitude. Don't let the flag I planted be pulled down."

There is unlikely to be a flag-posting ceremony this time but the fans will no doubt find something else to get agitated about in what is one of the most eagerly-awaited events in the Turkish sporting calendar.
